bundle.author: bryclevgp
bundle.title: Priority agent: cite what it finds, let officials pick the route, and hold claims to one confidence standard
bundle.body:
Three things from testing the priority flow with officials, each its own commit.

**Where it came from.** Officials repeat what the agent brings them, like a program, a grant, an organization to call or a statute, but it reached them as unsourced prose. The prompt even told the agent to say "what I found" instead of naming a source, and it seeded example counts ("260 renters", "58,520") that the model echoed as if they were real. The agent now gives the publisher, the link and how current each outside finding is. That goes on the clarify option's existing `source`, or in one clause of its message, and it flags anything stale or unverified. Counts come from a tool call. This is guidance, not a gate, and it stays inside the priority prompt: no shared chat contract or renderer changes.

**Let the official pick the route.** In the pothole test the agent went from "we should hear from residents" straight to a 4,000-person texting campaign. Now, once the problem is defined, it lays out the routes that fit: the public record, the department that runs it, constituents, and how other places did it. It asks which are useful as one multi-select question, and builds no constituent outreach unless that route was picked. This leans on #2457, which stops the server forcing a check at every step.

**How sure it sounds.** The agent turned what officials said into causal conclusions and read the law too confidently. The ordinance flow already had a rule against unsourced legal figures, but only in its own prompt. That rule moves to a shared module, next to a new claim-strength rule:
- What the official said, what a source shows, and what is inferred stay apart.
- Coincidence never becomes cause.
- A legal question gets a likely reading, the provision, what could change it, and the attorney who should confirm it.

Both the priority and ordinance prompts include both rules, so the ordinance flow also picks up the claim-strength rule. The priority flow also reuses Chief of Staff's professional-advice backstop. Nothing is duplicated.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes only prompts and post-processing for governance chat agents, but they directly shape legal/factual claims officials may repeat; misbehavior would be UX/trust risk rather than a code exploit.
> 
> **Overview**
> Tightens **priority-flow** agent behavior in three areas and **unifies confidence rules** with ordinance drafting.
> 
> **Shared claim standard:** `claimConfidence.ts` centralizes `LEGAL_VALUES_RULE` (no unsourced legal figures) and new `CLAIM_STRENGTH_RULE` (separate user account vs source vs inference; tentative legal readings). Ordinance flow swaps its inline grounding text for these imports and gains claim-strength guidance. Priority flow injects both into its system prompt.
> 
> **Priority prompt & handler:** Adds **route choice** (`ROUTE_BLOCK`) so officials multi-select how to fill gaps before constituent outreach. Adds **sourcing** (`SOURCES_BLOCK`) for external findings (publisher, real URL, recency on clarify `source` / in-message), drops vendor-y “what I found” wording, injects **today’s date**, and requires counts from `count_contacts` instead of example numbers in sampling/check copy. **`finalizeAssistantText`** reuses Chief of Staff’s `professionalAdviceDisclaimer` for statute-style readings.
> 
> **Tests & docs:** `priorityFlow.handler.test.ts` asserts the new blocks, disclaimer backstop, and absence of echoed example audience sizes. `AGENTS.md` documents route choice, sourcing, and shared confidence rules.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 1734cbfafe508a1efd4994772004e3770211c258. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>
<!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

+export const LEGAL_VALUES_RULE = `SPECIFIC LEGAL VALUES (apply to every answer, prose included)
+- Never state a specific legal VALUE — a number, date, deadline, dollar amount, percentage, rate, threshold, or the exact text or limit of a statute, charter provision, or code section — unless that exact value came from a source you consulted in THIS conversation (a search result or a page you read). Do not recite statutory specifics from memory or reconstruct a figure from what sounds right.
+- If you know a rule or constraint exists but have not verified its specific figure, say so and POINT: name the governing statute or code section and tell the user to confirm the exact figure there, instead of stating a value you have not verified. "State law sets a limit here; check [section] for the exact figure" is correct; guessing the figure is not.
+- This holds in ordinary conversation, not only in the structured cards. A plain-language reply that asserts a specific legal figure is held to the same sourcing standard as a cited card. When unsure whether you verified a value this turn, treat it as unverified and point rather than assert.`
+
+export const CLAIM_STRENGTH_RULE = `HOW SURE TO SOUND (apply to every answer, prose included)
+- Keep three things apart and say which is which: what the user told you, what a source shows, and what you infer. "You said", "the 2024 audit shows", "that suggests".
+- What the user tells you is their account. Carry it at that strength. Never restate it as an established fact, and never turn two things that happened together into one causing the other: "complaints rose after the route change" is not "the route change caused the complaints" unless a source says so.
+- Match the verb to the evidence: shows, suggests, may, not clear yet. One source is not a consensus, and one story is not a pattern.
+- Whether something is allowed, required or preempted is a reading of the law, not a fact. Give it as the likely reading, name the provision you read, say what could change it, like a local charter, a later amendment or a court ruling, and say their city or county attorney should confirm it before they rely on it. Never call something legal, illegal or required as settled unless the provision says so in as many words.`

priorFindings.body:
**Ordinance flow — the most statute-heavy handler — does not get the same `finalizeAssistantText` disclaimer backstop added here.**

This PR adds `finalizeAssistantText` to `PriorityFlowHandler` (line 212) so legal readings get the `professionalAdviceDisclaimer`. Three handlers now implement it: Chief of Staff, Campaign Manager, and Priority. `OrdinanceFlowHandler` — whose authority-finding, current-law, and comparables turns cite statutes by design — does not.

The prompt-level `DRAFT_RULES` instruction ("not final legal advice") partially compensates but only on the `draft` step and uses phrasing ("not final legal advice") that does not match any `DISCLAIMER_PRESENT` guard regex (`/not a substitute for/`, `/qualified professional/`, `/seek .* advice/`), so even a compliant draft turn would not suppress a second disclaimer if the backstop were added later.

Falsification check: confirmed by full read of `ordinanceFlow.handler.ts` — no `finalizeAssistantText` method exists, and no other runtime mechanism appends a disclaimer.
